blocks.text: NMR spectroscopy is based on the magnetic property (nuclear spin) of some nuclei. Nuclei such as hydrogen (1H) and carbon-13 (13C) behave like tiny magnets. With no magnetic field, all such nuclei point randomly and have the same energy. In a strong magnetic field they line up either with the field or against it, giving two spin states: a lower-energy state and a higher-energy state.

Radio waves of the right energy make nuclei in the lower state absorb energy and move to the higher state (spin flipping). When they return they give out energy, which is detected and turned into an NMR spectrum. The exact energy needed to flip a nucleus depends on its position in the compound and the atoms around it, together called its molecular environment. So NMR can tell apart hydrogen atoms in different environments in one molecule: in methanol, CH3OH, the three hydrogens on carbon and the one on oxygen absorb different energies. In practice, nuclei in different environments can be flipped with radio waves of a fixed frequency by varying the strength of the magnetic field.

blocks.alt: Left: an energy diagram; with no field, several spinning nuclei point randomly at one energy; with a field the level splits into a lower 'with field' state and a higher 'against field' state, and an arrow shows a radio wave being absorbed as a spin flips. Right: methanol, with the three hydrogens on carbon in blue and the O-H hydrogen in red.
blocks.caption: Spin states in a magnetic field, and two proton environments in methanol (original diagram after Figure 30.1).
blocks.long_description: A magnetic field splits the spin states of the nuclei into two energies. A nucleus absorbs a radio wave only when its energy matches the gap, and the gap depends slightly on the electrons around the nucleus, so differently placed hydrogens absorb at slightly different positions.

blocks.title: Did you know?
blocks.text: Nuclei with even numbers of both protons and neutrons, such as 12C, have their nuclear spins paired, so they have no overall magnetic field and give no NMR signal.

blocks.prompt: Why can NMR distinguish the hydrogen atoms of the CH3 group from the one in the OH group of methanol?
blocks.explanation: They are in different environments (bonded to C or to O), so the energy needed to flip their spins is different.

items: 1H and 13C nuclei act as magnets; in a field they have two spin states.
Radio waves flip spins; the energy depends on the environment.
